blocks.text: A Dream of Adventure

My name is Edward Malone, and at the time this story began I was a young reporter on the Daily Gazette in London. I was twenty-three, full of energy, and certain that a great life was waiting for me. The problem was that I had no idea how to begin it.

There was also Gladys Hungerton. I admired her more than anyone I had ever met, and one evening I finally asked her to marry me. She did not laugh at me or become angry. Instead, she looked serious and told me that she valued our friendship but did not love me in the way I hoped.

Gladys said "I love a man who has done something brave. Someone who has faced danger, traveled into the unknown, and proved that he can act when it matters." I tried to joke. "So I must discover a new country before you will consider me?" "Not for me," she replied. "If a man is truly brave, he does not act just to impress someone else. He acts because courage is part of his character." Her words stayed with me. I left her house feeling disappointed, but also strangely
excited.
London suddenly seemed too safe. I wanted a challenge - something that would test me and give my life a clearer purpose.

The next evening I went straight to my editor, Mr McArdle. He was an experienced newspaper man who had seen every kind of young reporter. When I asked him to send me on a dangerous assignment, he pushed his glasses up and stared at me.

"You want danger?" he said. "Most sensible people want to avoid it." "I want a real story, sir. Something difficult." He studied me for a moment, then smiled. "Perhaps I do have a job for you. blocks.text: Professor Challenger's Secret
Professor Challenger began by asking me questions
about the scientific article I had mentioned in my letter.
At first I tried to answer confidently, but the questions became more technical every minute.
"And what do you think of the recent evidence?" he asked. "Very interesting," I said carefully.
"Which evidence?" I hesitated.

His eyes narrowed. "You know nothing about this subject." There was no point pretending any longer. "Very little, " I admitted. "Then why are you here?" I took a breath. "I am a reporter for the Daily Gazette." For one silent second, nothing happened. Then Challenger rose from his chair like a storm. "A journalist!

In my house!" He came towards me. I told him firmly not to touch me. He ignored the warning. A moment later we were struggling in the hallway, crashing into a chair and rolling through the open front door. We landed together on the steps outside.
A policeman hurried over. Several neighbors stopped to watch. "What happened?" the policeman asked.

My eye was beginning to swell, and Challenger's coat was torn. I could easily have made a complaint. Instead, I remembered that I had entered his house under a false name and had deliberately tricked him.
"It was partly my fault," I said. "I will not press charges." The policeman looked surprised, but closed his notebook.
Challenger stared at me. The anger in his face changed into something almost like respect.

blocks.text: Into the Unknown

Lord John had hired a steam launch called the Esmeralda to carry us up the Amazon. The river was so wide that, even far inland, the opposite bank often looked like a distant shadow. Day after day we moved through heat, rain, brilliant sunlight, and walls of green forest.

Challenger refused to reveal our exact route. He made all of us promise that, even if we returned safely, we would not publish enough information for strangers to locate the plateau. He said careless visitors could destroy a place that science had barely discovered.
After several days we left the main river and entered a large tributary. It gradually became narrower. At a small riverside village, Challenger ordered the Esmeralda back to Manaos.
“From here we use canoes,” he said. “Soon there will be rapids. A steam launch cannot continue.” We hired two local guides who had accompanied Challenger during his earlier journey.
They were clearly frightened by the idea of returning, but they knew the route.

For several days our canoes moved through a beautiful green waterway. Monkeys watched us from branches. Bright birds stood on fallen logs. Once we saw a puma disappear into the forest. The animals seemed less afraid of humans the farther we traveled.
Then the water became too shallow. We hid the canoes and continued on foot, carrying food, rifles, blankets, instruments, and medical supplies.

The land rose steadily. Thick tropical forest gave way to palms, rocky slopes, orchids, bamboo, and wide areas of tree-ferns. Progress was exhausting. Sometimes we spent an entire day cutting a path through bamboo so dense that we could see only a few meters ahead.
Challenger and Summerlee argued constantly.
“We should follow the compass,” Challenger insisted one morning.

My companions were pleased with what I had seen from the tree. That evening, by the light of our fire, I drew a rough map of the plateau. We marked the cliff where we had entered, the forest, the pterodactyl swamp, and the large lake in the center.
“The man who first saw the lake should name it,” Lord John said. I thought of Gladys and the reason I had first wanted adventure. “Lake Gladys,” I said.

Summerlee gave me a dry look, but Challenger nodded. “Lake Gladys it is.” I should have been satisfied with the day’s work. Instead, I became restless. I wanted to prove that I could contribute more than notes and maps. I also wanted to examine the signs of human life near the far side of the lake.
That night, after the others were asleep, I took a rifle, some food, and a small electric lamp.
I left Fort Challenger alone.
At first the forest was peaceful. Moonlight appeared through gaps in the leaves.
I followed the stream, using the map in my head. The farther I traveled, the more foolish my decision seemed, but pride kept me moving.
After several hours I reached the lake.
Its surface reflected the moon. For a few minutes I forgot the danger and simply watched.
Then a heavy shape moved near the water.
An enormous stegosaurus stepped into the open.
I recognized it immediately from Maple White’s drawing. Plates rose along its back, and spikes extended from its tail. It lowered its head to drink, completely unaware of me.
I wanted to shout with excitement, but I remained still. This was living proof of a world that should have disappeared millions of years ago.
Then the stegosaurus suddenly lifted its head. It had heard something.

blocks.text: The Battle for the Plateau

The Accala force moved towards the forest in a long line. Scouts went ahead, while the main group followed with bows and spears. Lord John and Summerlee took the right side. Challenger and I moved on the left.
No one spoke much. Even Challenger seemed to understand that this was not a scientific demonstration.
The first attack came suddenly.

A group of ape-men rushed from the trees, swinging heavy clubs and throwing stones. The Accala were faster. They moved aside, fired arrows and spears, and surrounded the attackers before they could break the line.
The battle became more dangerous inside the forest.

Ape-men dropped from branches. Others charged from behind bushes. Their strength was enormous. One blow broke Summerlee’s rifle. An Accala warrior pulled him away before another strike could reach him.
Our rifles gave the Accala an important advantage, but we used them only when the fighting came close. Lord John moved calmly from one position to another, never wasting a shot.
After more than an hour, the ape-men began to retreat. The Accala followed.
